transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah, thanks. Um, well, so I'm twenty-one, and I just finished my bachelor's degree, which is great, you know, but now I'm in that phase where I'm applying for everything—jobs, internships, grad school, you name it. And, well, what finally made me come in, what really just broke the camel's back, I guess, is that I keep turning in these applications, or even my research notes from my last semester, with these small but just incredibly embarrassing mistakes. I mean, I'm talking about things like mislabeling the date on a piece of artwork in my portfolio, which is a huge deal in art history, or completely skipping a question on an application form. And the thing is, the really frustrating part, is that I honestly thought I had checked them. I mean, I sit there, and I look over the document, and I tell myself, "Okay, I'm reading this, I'm checking for errors," and I genuinely believe I've caught everything. But then I submit it, and someone points out this glaring mistake, and I just feel so stupid. It's like my brain just glosses over the details, no matter how hard I try to focus on them. I've tried reading things out loud, I've tried changing the font, I've tried everything I can think of, but it just keeps happening, and it's really starting to affect my confidence, you know? Like, how am I supposed to get a job if I can't even fill out a form correctly? It's just... it's exhausting, honestly.
Do you find yourself making these kinds of mistakes or feeling this level of anxiety in other areas of your life, outside of applying for jobs or school?

Um, honestly... not really? Or, at least, I haven't really noticed it happening in other areas. I mean, if I think about my day-to-day life right now, especially since I'm not working and just kind of living at home while I figure things out, there isn't really a lot of opportunity to make those kinds of high-stakes mistakes, I guess. 

Like, if I'm hanging out with my friends or, I don't know, playing video games or just reading, it doesn't really matter if I gloss over a detail. Nobody is grading me on how I load the dishwasher, you know? And even when I was living in my own apartment last year for my senior year, sure, maybe I'd occasionally forget to buy milk at the grocery store or something, but that's just normal, right? Everyone does that. That doesn't give me this... this massive pit in my stomach like the applications do. Because if I forget milk, I just go back to the store. No harm, no foul. But if I mess up an internship application, that's it, the door is closed, they think I'm careless and unprofessional. 

So, yeah, I don't really feel that anxiety when I'm just going about my normal day, and I don't think I'm making those kinds of glaring, embarrassing errors when I'm just doing my hobbies or running errands. It really just seems completely isolated to these forms and documents and things where I have to sit down and be perfectly accurate. I just don't get why my brain decides to kind of just shut off exactly when I need it to be sharpest, but yeah, outside of the job hunt and the school stuff, I'd say I haven't really noticed anything like that.
Do you find yourself repeatedly checking things, like locks or appliances, when you're not filling out applications or documents?

No, um, I really don't do that at all. Like, if we're talking about the front door or the stove, I never really go back and check them. Actually, since I moved back in with my parents after graduation, my dad is usually the one who locks up the house at night anyway. He has this whole routine where he walks around at like ten o'clock, making sure the deadbolts are thrown and the garage is shut, so I don't even have to think about the locks right now. But even when I had my own apartment last year for my senior year, I would just lock the door when I left for class and that was it. I never had that sudden panic of wondering if I locked it, where you have to walk all the way back up three flights of stairs just to jiggle the handle. I just locked it and walked away. 

And it's the exact same with appliances, too. I mean, I might heat up a frozen pizza or make some pasta or something, and I just turn the oven off when the timer goes off, and I don't really give it a second thought after that. I definitely don't stand there staring at the stove, checking the dials over and over to make sure the little line is pointing to off. It's actually kind of funny you ask that, because my old roommate used to do exactly that with his clothes iron. He would get halfway to campus and then turn around because he was convinced he left it plugged in and was going to burn the building down, but it was always unplugged. I always felt bad for him because it looked so stressful. 

But for me? No, never. My brain doesn't get stuck on those physical things around the house. It's really just the reading and the writing and the applications where I feel like I have to review things, and even then, I'm not checking it fifty times in a row, I'm just trying to read it through carefully to catch the mistakes, and I still somehow miss them. So yeah, locks and stoves and household stuff, that is definitely not an issue for me at all.
Do you often find yourself worrying about everyday things, like money or relationships, even when there's no apparent reason to worry?

Um, no, not really. I mean, I don't think so. Like, with money, for example... I mean, obviously, I don't have a job right now, which is exactly why I'm doing all these applications, but I'm not, like, sitting up at night agonizing over my bank account. Because, well, I'm living at home with my parents, like I mentioned earlier, and they're being really great about it. They aren't charging me rent or making me pay for utilities or anything right now, which is a huge privilege, I know. I just pay for my own gas and, you know, if I want to go out with friends or buy a video game or something, I use the savings I have from my campus job last year. So there's no real pressure there, no impending doom about making rent or buying groceries. If I was living on my own right now and the clock was ticking on my savings, maybe I'd be an absolute wreck, but right now? No, I don't really worry about money just out of the blue. 

And as for relationships... honestly, no to that, too. I have a pretty solid group of friends from college. A lot of them scattered after graduation, you know, moving back to their own hometowns or going off to grad school in other states, which was kind of a bummer, but we have this huge group chat on Discord where we talk pretty much every single day. We play games online a few nights a week, so we're still really connected. I never really get that feeling of, like, wondering if they're mad at me or if I said something wrong. If someone's quiet for a few days, I just assume they're busy with their own job hunt or just dealing with post-grad life. 

And I'm not dating anyone right now, so there's no relationship drama to stress over either. My last relationship ended pretty amicably back in the fall of my senior year—we just kind of realized we were going in different directions after graduation, so there was no big messy fallout to overthink or obsess over. 

So, yeah, I don't really sit around worrying about that kind of everyday stuff unless there's a really obvious, glaring reason to. Like I was saying before, all my stress, all that awful anxious energy, it's just entirely funneled into these applications and the fear of making a stupid typo that ruins my chances. That's the only thing that really gets under my skin and makes me panic. The rest of my life is actually pretty low-stress right now, all things considered. I just kind of take things as they come when I'm not staring at a cover letter.
Do you think you would still feel anxious about making mistakes on applications if you were already securely employed?

Um, wow, that’s... I mean, I guess I’ve never really thought about it like that, because right now the pressure just feels so heavy, you know? But if I really think about it... if I already had a job, like, say I was already securely employed at some firm or whatever, working a normal nine-to-five and making a steady paycheck... I don't think I'd have this same level of panic. 

I mean, sure, I'd probably still be annoyed with myself if I made a typo, because nobody *likes* looking careless, right? It’s always embarrassing when you realize you used the wrong "their" or left out a whole word in a sentence after you already hit submit. But that massive, awful pit in my stomach? The feeling that my whole future is riding on this one single PDF document? I really don't think that would be there. 

Because right now, the stakes just feel incredibly high. Every application feels like a literal lifeline. Even though my parents are being super supportive about me living at home, like I was saying before, I still feel this ticking clock in my head. I want to start my life, get my own place again, prove that my degree was actually worth all the time and effort. So when I sit down to fill out a form, my brain is just screaming, "Don't mess this up, this is your one shot!" And then, of course, I get so worked up that I end up glossing over a detail or making a mistake anyway. 

But if I already had a job? If I was just applying for, I don't know, a different role, or maybe looking to pivot to a different company just to see what’s out there? The stakes would be so much lower. If I messed up an application and they rejected me, I’d just wake up the next day and go to my regular job. I’d still have an income. I wouldn’t be stuck in my childhood bedroom trying to figure out my life. So, yeah, I think the anxiety is really tied to the fact that I absolutely *need* this to work out right now. If I had that security net already under me, I’d probably just fill the forms out, check them over, and send them off without feeling like I was defusing a bomb. It's just the current situation that makes every little mistake feel so completely catastrophic, I think.
Do you feel like you need to be perfect in all aspects of your life, not just when it comes to applications and documents?

Oh, definitely not. No way. Honestly, if you saw my bedroom right now, you would probably laugh out loud at the idea of me being a perfectionist. I mean, my mom is actually constantly on my case about it because I have clean laundry piled up on this chair in the corner of my room—you know, that one chair everyone has that just inevitably becomes the clothes chair? Yeah, mine is basically a mountain at this point. I just dig through it when I need a shirt instead of actually folding it and putting it in the dresser. And my desk is just covered in half-empty water bottles and old mail I haven't sorted through. I really don't care if things are messy or just "good enough" in my day-to-day life. 

Like, even with my hobbies, I'm absolutely not a perfectionist. When I play video games with my friends on Discord, like I was talking about earlier, I'm usually the one making goofy mistakes and just laughing it off. I'm not trying to min-max my stats or be the absolute best, most flawless player on the server. I just play to have fun. And with cooking—well, I mentioned I usually just make frozen pizza and pasta, but on the rare occasion I actually try to cook a real meal, if I burn the edges of the chicken or put in way too much pepper, I just eat it anyway. I don't throw it out and start over in a panic. It's just food, you know? It doesn't have to be a Michelin-star experience. I don't even iron my shirts unless I have a Zoom interview! 

So, yeah, this whole intense, agonizing need to get everything exactly one hundred percent right... it's literally just the job applications and the resumes. It's like my brain has this one tiny, specific box labeled "Things That Must Be Flawless" and the only thing inside it is my job hunt. Everything else in my life? I'm totally fine with it being average, or messy, or just getting by. I definitely don't have that exhausting drive to be perfect across the board. It's really just the professional stuff right now that makes me feel like I have to be completely error-free.
Do you think you would feel anxious about making mistakes if you were in a situation where the stakes were high, but it wasn't related to job applications or your professional future?

High stakes but not jobs... um, man, I'm trying to even picture what that would look like right now. Because, honestly, my brain is just so completely saturated with employment stuff that it's hard to even imagine a high-stakes scenario that doesn't involve a hiring manager, you know? Like... what would that even be? 

I guess if you mean something like, I don't know, a medical emergency? Like if I had to drive a friend to the emergency room in the middle of a blizzard or something crazy like that. If I was in that situation, yeah, I'd probably be absolutely terrified of making a mistake, like taking a wrong turn or skidding on the ice. But I feel like literally anyone would be anxious in that scenario, right? That's just basic human survival instinct kicking in, not really the same weird, paralyzing dread I get over whether I used a semicolon correctly in a cover letter. 

But if you mean high stakes like... maybe planning a massive event, or handling a huge sum of money for a club, or something like that? I just haven't really had to do anything like that. The highest stakes thing I do outside of applying for jobs is probably, like I was saying earlier, playing those online games with my friends. And even if we're doing a really difficult raid and everyone's counting on me to not mess up my role, and maybe people get a little annoyed if we wipe and have to start over... it's still just a game. Nobody's life is ruined. The server resets, we try again. So I don't get that awful pit in my stomach. 

So, yeah, honestly, I'm really not sure. I haven't been in a non-professional high-stakes situation anytime recently to even compare it to. Ever since I walked across that stage at graduation, my entire universe has just shrunk down to my laptop screen, my childhood bedroom, and job boards. It's like my whole reality is just this one specific bubble. I guess I just don't have a good point of reference right now to say whether I'd freak out about mistakes in some other major life event, because I'm just not experiencing any other major life events right now. I mean, maybe I would? But it's really hard to say without actually being in the moment, you know what I mean?
Do you think your anxiety about making mistakes on applications is related to the fear of what others will think of you?

Um, what others think of me? Like, being judged? I don't... I don't really think so. I mean, if I really break it down and think about who the "others" even are in this situation, it just doesn't track for me. 

Because if you mean the people actually reading the applications—the recruiters, or the hiring managers, or whoever is sitting on the other side of the Taleo portal—I don't even know them. They're basically just faceless email addresses to me, you know? Like, half the time it's just an automated "careers at whatever dot com" address anyway. If I send them a cover letter with a typo and some HR person in an office three states away thinks, "Wow, this kid is an idiot," I mean... I'll never meet them. I'll never pass them on the street. It's not like high school or college where if you do something embarrassing in a presentation, everyone in the cafeteria knows about it the next day and you have to actually face them. A random recruiter thinking I'm careless doesn't really hurt my feelings on a personal level at all. 

And if you mean people in my actual real life, like my friends or my parents? It's definitely not them either. Like I said before, my parents are being incredibly supportive about the whole living-at-home thing. They aren't sitting around judging me or thinking I'm a failure because I haven't landed a job yet. My mom is always just checking in to make sure I'm not stressing myself out too much, and my dad is constantly sending me articles about how tough the entry-level job market is right now, almost like he's trying to make sure I know it's not my fault. And my friends from my degree program? Half of them are in the exact same boat as me anyway. They're also back in their hometowns, living in their old bedrooms, getting the same automated rejection emails. We actually joke about it a lot. We have this group chat where we send screenshots of the most ridiculous, out-of-touch application requirements we find, or the fastest rejection emails we get. So I'm definitely not worried about my friends thinking less of me, because we're all kind of mutually struggling.

So, no, honestly, it's really not about my reputation or caring if people think I'm smart or capable. It's literally just the practical consequences. If I make a mistake, my application gets thrown in the trash. If it goes in the trash, I don't get an interview. If I don't get an interview, I don't get a job, and I'm stuck in this holding pattern for another six months, staring at the exact same glow-in-the-dark stars on my ceiling that I stuck up there when I was twelve years old. That's what actually terrifies me. It's the fear of being stuck and not being able to start my actual adult life. It has nothing to do with somebody sitting at a desk somewhere thinking poorly of my grammar, I just really, really need a paycheck so I can move out.
Do you think you would feel anxious about making mistakes in general if your current job hunt and living situation were resolved?

Man, if my job hunt and living situation were just... resolved? Like, if I actually had a job and my own apartment? Honestly, I really, really doubt I'd be anxious about making mistakes in general. I mean, I can't say for one hundred percent certain because, obviously, I'm not in that situation right now, but just thinking about it... if I had a steady paycheck coming in and I was finally out of my childhood bedroom, I think this massive weight would just completely lift off my shoulders. 

Like I was saying before about my messy room and how I just mess around in video games with my friends, I'm naturally a pretty laid-back guy. I don't usually stress about the little things at all. It's literally just this one massive, looming cloud of 'you need to start your adult life' that's making me obsess over every single comma and bullet point on my applications. If I was just going to work every day, doing whatever entry-level tasks they gave me... I mean, sure, I wouldn't want to mess up and get fired, obviously, but I really don't think I'd have this paralyzing fear of a single mistake ruining my future, you know? Because I'd already have my foot in the door. I'd be established. 

I could just go to work, do my job, come home to my own place, maybe cook one of those frozen pizzas I mentioned earlier, and just relax. It sounds so incredibly nice just picturing it, honestly. Just having a normal Tuesday where my biggest problem is, I don't know, forgetting to buy milk at the grocery store, instead of wondering if I used the wrong font size on a cover letter and doomed my entire career trajectory. So, yeah, I really don't think the anxiety would stick around. It feels entirely tied to just needing to escape this weird limbo phase I'm stuck in right now.
Do you think you would feel anxious about making mistakes if the task was very important to you, but not related to your job or professional future?

I mean, I think this kind of circles back to what we were talking about a few minutes ago, right? With the whole high-stakes thing. Because if a task was just... personally really important to me, but had absolutely nothing to do with my career or getting out of my parents' house? I honestly don't think I'd have that same kind of anxiety. I mean, I really haven't noticed myself getting freaked out over personal stuff at all. 

Like, okay, let's say hypothetically I was building a custom gaming PC. I've actually thought about doing that if I ever get some money together. That would be a huge deal to me, super important, because the parts are crazy expensive. And if you mess up—like, if you accidentally bend a pin on the motherboard or fry the processor—that's hundreds of dollars just instantly down the drain. So, sure, in the exact ten seconds I'm dropping the chip into the socket, I might be a little nervous. But I wouldn't be sitting there for three days beforehand, totally paralyzed, staring at the thermal paste and terrified to make a move, you know? I'd just watch a YouTube tutorial, take a breath, and do it. 

Because even if the absolute worst happened and I ruined the PC, it's just a thing. It would suck, I'd be mad at myself, but my life wouldn't be over. It wouldn't mean I'm trapped in my childhood bedroom for another year. The anxiety I'm dealing with right now is just so incredibly specific to this feeling of my entire existence being on pause. If a task is just "important to me"—like a hobby, or organizing a trip for my friends, or something like that—I don't get that suffocating dread about making a mistake. I've always been a pretty "go with the flow" guy in my actual personal life. If we take a wrong turn on a road trip, we just take the next exit, no big deal. 

So, yeah, I really don't think I'd be anxious like that. But again, it's almost hard to even separate the two right now, because getting a job is literally the only important thing in my life at this exact moment. Everything else is just kind of background noise while I wait for my life to actually start.
Do you think you would feel anxious about failing at something if it wasn't related to your job search or professional development?

I mean, honestly, no. Not at all. And I feel like that's pretty much what we were just talking about, right? Because failing at something that doesn't have those massive stakes... I mean, who cares? I fail at stuff all the time and it doesn't bother me in the slightest. 

Like, okay, in those video games I was telling you about that I play with my friends? We play a lot of these competitive squad-based shooters, and sometimes I just completely blow the match for us. Like, I'll miss a ridiculously easy shot, or I'll walk right into an obvious trap, and we lose the whole round entirely because of me. That's a failure, technically, right? And my friends will absolutely roast me for it in the voice chat, they'll be like, "Dude, what were you even looking at?" But I don't get anxious about it beforehand, and I don't stress about it after. I just laugh it off, we queue up for the next match, and it's completely forgotten five minutes later. 

Because what happens if I fail in the game? My digital rank goes down a little bit. Big deal. Or, like, what happens if I try to learn to cook something new and I completely burn it? I just throw it away and make a sandwich. It doesn't actually impact my life. I don't have this... this deep-seated fear of failure as a concept, you know? I'm really not a perfectionist. I don't need to be the best at everything I do, or even good at it, honestly. I just need to get out of my parents' house. 

So, yeah, if it's not related to my career or making money so I can finally sign a lease somewhere, failure just doesn't register as a threat to me. It's just a normal part of doing stuff. I really think my brain only hits that panic button when my actual, real-life future is on the line. If there's no real-world consequence to messing up, I'm totally fine with falling flat on my face.
Do you think you would feel anxious about failing at something if it had significant consequences, but wasn't related to your job search or professional development?

Significant consequences... man, I'm trying to even think of what that would look like in my life right now. Because, like, if it's not my job search or my career, what else actually has genuinely significant consequences for me at twenty-one? 

I guess... I don't know, let's say I was driving my dad's car. He has this really nice truck that he basically treats like his third child, and let's say I had to drive it on the highway in the middle of a massive snowstorm. If I mess up and crash that, the consequences are huge, right? The truck is totaled, my dad would absolutely kill me, insurance goes through the roof, maybe I get seriously hurt. So, in the moment? Yeah, obviously I'd be careful. I'd be gripping the steering wheel pretty tight and paying attention. But I wouldn't be sitting in my room for a week beforehand, completely paralyzed by the dread of driving, terrified that I'm inherently a failure as a driver and that I'm going to ruin my life. I'd just get in the car, drive slow, and deal with it.

Or, like, what if one of my best friends was going through a massive personal crisis and really, really needed me to be there for them? Like, a life-or-death kind of emotional support situation. If I fail at that, if I say the completely wrong thing or I'm not a good friend, I could lose that friendship forever. That's a huge, significant consequence. But I wouldn't feel *anxious* about failing at it in this same suffocating way. I'd just... go over to their house, bring them some food, and listen. I wouldn't be drafting what I was going to say to them on a notepad and agonizing over every single word the way I do when I'm writing an email to a recruiter. 

So, honestly? No. I really, genuinely don't think I'd have that specific kind of anxiety. It's like... I feel like my brain only has a limited capacity for this kind of intense, paralyzing panic, and right now, one hundred percent of that capacity is taken up by the fact that I have a bachelor's degree and I'm still sleeping in a twin bed with posters I put up in high school on the walls. I just haven't noticed myself getting paralyzed by the fear of failure in literally any other context, no matter how high the stakes supposedly are. It really is just this one massive, specific hurdle. I don't walk around terrified of failing at life in general, I just... I just really need to get my life started, you know? Everything else I can handle just fine.
Do you think your anxiety about making mistakes on applications is related to a fear of being evaluated or judged by others, rather than just the practical consequences of not getting a job?

I mean, not really? Like, I don't think it's about being judged at all, honestly. Because when you really think about it, who is even looking at these applications? 

Half the time, I'm pretty sure it's not even a human being. It's just those, um, those ATS things—the applicant tracking software algorithms that just scan your PDF for keywords and instantly toss you into the digital trash can if you didn't use the exact right corporate buzzwords. You can't really fear the judgment of a computer program, you know? It's just a machine. 

And even if a real, actual person is reading it—like some HR recruiter sitting in a cubicle somewhere in another state—I don't know them. I'm never going to meet them. If they look at my cover letter and think, "Wow, this guy writes like a complete idiot," or "Why did he format his margins like this, what a loser," I genuinely do not care what their personal opinion of me is. It's not like high school where you're standing up in front of the class and you're terrified everyone is going to laugh at you. It's a completely faceless, totally impersonal transaction. 

If I could somehow get the job, but the catch was that the hiring manager thought I was the most pathetic, embarrassing person on earth, I would take that deal in a heartbeat. I really would. Because their opinion of me doesn't matter. What matters is the math of the situation. If they judge my resume as bad, they hit the "reject" button. If they hit "reject," I don't get an interview. If I don't get the interview, I don't get the job. And if I don't get the job, I'm still waking up tomorrow morning in the exact same room I've been in since I was a kid, walking downstairs, and having to listen to my mom ask me if I've "put myself out there today" while I'm just trying to eat my cereal. 

That's the terrifying part. The absolute, soul-crushing reality of the practical consequences. The fear is just about being stuck in this sort of... this purgatory, I guess. I just want a paycheck and an apartment with my own name on the lease. So, yeah, the evaluation part of it? The judgment? It's literally just a mechanical roadblock to the practical part. I don't lose any sleep over what some random recruiter thinks of me as a person. I just care that they hold the keys to me actually starting my life.
Do you think you would feel anxious about failing at something that has nothing to do with your job search or professional life, but is still very important to you?

I mean, I feel like I'm repeating myself a little bit here, but... no. Not at all. I really don't. 

Because... okay, if I try to think about what is actually, genuinely important to me right now outside of getting a job and finally moving out... honestly, it's hard to even separate anything else out, because that one single goal is just eating up my entire existence. But, okay, let's say... my hobbies. The things I do with my friends. Like, I've been running this massive Dungeons and Dragons campaign for my main group of friends. I'm the Dungeon Master, and I've spent, I don't know, probably eighty or ninety hours over the last few months just world-building this entire continent. I've been drawing out these ridiculously detailed maps, writing all this deep lore for the different political factions, coming up with backstories... it's incredibly important to me. I care about it a lot. I want my friends to have an amazing time, and I want the story we're telling to be genuinely good. 

But if we sit down on a Friday night and the session just completely flops? Like, say they completely ignore all my plot hooks, the combat encounter I planned is super boring, and I completely mess up the rules and ruin the pacing. I don't feel that crushing, paralyzing panic about it. I might be a little bummed out, sure. I might think, "Man, I really dropped the ball on that one, that kind of sucked." But I don't get *anxious* about it beforehand, and I don't spiral about it after. I don't sit there staring at my notebook for three days, terrified to plan the next session because I'm so scared of messing up again. I just figure out what went wrong and try to do better next week. 

I just... I don't have that reaction. It's like my brain fundamentally knows that even if I completely fail at this thing I really, truly care about, my actual life isn't on the line. 

I really feel like we keep trying to find this deep-rooted, overarching fear of failure in me, and I'm trying to tell you, it's just not there. I'm not a fragile person when it comes to caring about things. It really is just the practical reality of being twenty-one, having a degree I spent four years of my life getting, and having absolutely nothing to show for it. If you took the job hunt away—like, if you just magically handed me a decent entry-level job tomorrow—I swear to you, all of this anxiety would vanish instantly. I wouldn't suddenly start stressing about failing at my hobbies or failing at being a good friend or anything else that's important to me. I'd just be a normal guy who finally has his own apartment.
Do you think you would feel anxious about failing at something that has significant consequences, but is not related to your job search or professional development?

Wait, didn't you... I feel like you just asked me this almost exact same question a few minutes ago, right? About the significant consequences outside of the job hunt? Like I said with my dad's truck earlier, or the hypothetical thing with my friend... I really, truly do not get paralyzed by that kind of stuff. 

I mean, maybe I'm not explaining myself clearly, or maybe you're looking for some specific hidden, overarching panic thing that I'm just not giving you, but I promise, I'm being completely honest here. I don't sit around worrying about crashing cars or ruining friendships or, I don't know, accidentally burning the house down if I leave the stove on. Obviously, if the house burned down, the consequences would be catastrophic, right? We'd lose everything, my parents would be devastated, we'd have nowhere to live. It doesn't get more significant than that. But I don't stand in the kitchen staring at the stove for twenty minutes, sweating and hyperventilating, terrified that I'm going to turn the dial the wrong way and ruin our lives. I just cook my eggs, turn the burner off, and go eat. 

It's just... my brain doesn't do that. The only thing that makes my chest tight and makes me want to crawl out of my skin is the fact that I'm twenty-one, I've sent out probably two hundred resumes in the last three months, and I'm still having to ask my mom for twenty bucks if I want to go get a burger with my friends. That's the only consequence that actually haunts me, because it's actually happening right now. So, yeah, no. I really don't have that kind of anxiety about anything else. I honestly don't know how else to say it, it's just the job stuff.
Do you think you would feel anxious about failing at something if there were no consequences at all, just the fact that you failed?

Okay, I... I really feel like you're trying to psychoanalyze a rock here. Like, no consequences at all? Just failing for the sake of failing? No. Zero anxiety. None whatsoever. 

Because... I mean, what does that even mean, really? Failing with no consequences. Like, if I'm sitting in my room playing a video game, right?
